title: Container Registry Security
summary: Container registry security covers the controls that protect the store where container images are pushed, pulled and promoted, from the registry service itself through to the proxy or mirror that build agents use. The asset at risk is not only the image layer contents but also the manifest, the tags and the repository namespaces, because anyone who can push to a repository your clusters pull from effectively controls what runs inside those clusters. In real environments the registry appears as a private registry behind single sign on, as a cloud provider registry with repository policies, and as signed image metadata that an admission controller verifies before a pod is scheduled. The common mistake is treating the registry as plain file storage, so teams enforce strong build time scanning but leave repository write access broad and tag mutability unlimited, which lets an attacker retag a known good image and inherit its trust.

beginner.definition: A container registry is the place where container images are stored and shared. It holds the picture of an application, called an image, and gives it a name and a version tag. Registry security means controlling who may add images, who may read them, and whether the images are genuine.
beginner.whyItMatters: Everything your platform runs starts as an image pulled from a registry. If someone can push an image into a repository your clusters trust, they can run their own code there. Many teams spend effort on scanning images but leave write access wide open. A stolen build password is then enough to replace a trusted image. Strong registry controls stop that path early.
howItWorks: A developer or build job logs into the registry using an account, a token, or a short lived certificate.
The registry checks that the account is allowed to push to that exact repository name.
Each image is stored as layers plus a manifest, and a tag such as latest points at one manifest.
Your cluster pulls the image, and an admission check confirms the image signature and scan result.
The registry keeps logs and scan records, so you can see who pushed what and when.
Old and unused images are removed on a schedule, which shrinks the attack surface.
beginner.example: Think of a public library with a locked back room. Anyone may borrow a book, but only approved staff may add a new book to the shelf. Each book has a label showing the shelf and the edition. If the back room door is left open, a stranger can slip in a fake book. It looks exactly like a trusted one, and readers will never notice. Registry security is the locked back room, the staff list, and the label check. It also includes the habit of checking the seal before the book goes on the shelf.
takeaways: Treat the registry as a trusted source of code, not as simple file storage.
Give push access only to the few accounts and build jobs that truly need it.
Check image signatures and scan results before your cluster runs an image.

objectives: Explain what a container registry is and why its contents are treated as trusted code.
Describe how repository permissions and image tags affect what a cluster will run.
Identify the controls that stop a registry becoming a distribution point for malicious images.
Recognise the common mistake of scanning images while leaving push access broad.
Outline how image signing and admission checks combine to protect a deployment.
